subject: design-technology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE D&T simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Identifying needs and writing a design brief

questions.q: Which phrase best describes an 'iterative' design process?
options: Designing only after the product has been manufactured
Copying an existing product exactly
A repeating cycle of designing, making and evaluating, improving the idea each time
Following each stage once, in a fixed order, to a final answer
questions.explain: Iterative design is a cyclic, repeating process: ideas are designed, modelled, tested and evaluated, then refined again and again until the solution meets the need.

questions.q: During prototyping a designer finds a fault, so they return to redevelop their ideas. This 'looping back' is a key feature of which approach?
options: Linear design
Iterative design
Mass production
Reverse engineering
questions.explain: Looping back to earlier stages to improve a design is exactly what makes a process iterative rather than a one-way linear sequence.

questions.lo: Identifying needs and writing a design brief
questions.q: What is the main purpose of a design brief?
options: To advertise the finished product to customers
To give a short outline of the problem and what the designer is being asked to do
To list the exact dimensions and materials of the final product
To record test results after making
questions.explain: A design brief is a short statement of the problem/need and what the client wants the designer to produce; the detailed measurable requirements come later in the specification.

questions.lo: Identifying needs and writing a design brief
questions.q: A charity needs a low-cost water carrier for children in rural areas. Identifying this problem and turning it into a starting statement is which stage of the design process?
options: Identifying a need and writing the brief
Prototyping
Manufacture
Evaluation
questions.explain: Recognising the problem/need and expressing it as a starting statement is the identifying-a-need and design-brief stage, right at the beginning of the process.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of PRIMARY research?
options: Carrying out a survey of potential users yourself
Studying a manufacturer's online datasheet
Looking up data in a textbook
Reading an existing product-review website
questions.explain: Primary research is first-hand data the designer gathers themselves, such as questionnaires, surveys and interviews. Textbooks and websites are secondary sources.

questions.q: A good design specification should be...
options: A set of clear, measurable points the product must meet
A drawing of the final idea
A list of only the tools needed
A single vague sentence
questions.explain: A specification lists specific, measurable criteria (size, cost, materials, function, safety) that the design must satisfy and against which it can later be tested.

questions.q: Which specification point is written in the most useful, testable way?
options: The product should be quite cheap
The product should look nice
The product should be a good size
The product must cost less than 5 dollars to make
questions.explain: 'Must cost less than 5 dollars' is specific and measurable, so it can be objectively tested. The others are vague and cannot be checked reliably.

questions.q: Why do designers usually generate several different ideas rather than just one?
options: To use up more paper
To copy competitors more easily
To explore a range of possible solutions before choosing and developing the best
Because the specification demands exactly ten ideas
questions.explain: Producing a range of ideas encourages creativity and lets the designer compare options against the specification before developing the strongest one.

questions.q: A quick, free-flowing method of producing many ideas rapidly, often in a group, is called...
options: Brainstorming (thought showering)
Quality control
Batch production
Anthropometrics
questions.explain: Brainstorming, or thought showering, rapidly generates many ideas without judging them at first, which is useful early in idea generation.

questions.q: 'Developing' an idea means...
options: Only colouring in the sketch neatly
Refining and improving a chosen idea, adding detail on materials, sizes and construction
Selling the idea to a client
Throwing the idea away and starting again
questions.explain: Development takes a chosen idea further, refining it with detail such as dimensions, materials, joints and function, often using annotated drawings and models.

questions.q: What is the main reason for making a model or prototype before full manufacture?
options: To sell it immediately
To avoid having to write a specification
To skip the evaluation stage
To test and evaluate how the design works and looks, so faults are found early
questions.explain: Modelling and prototyping let a designer test function, ergonomics and appearance and spot problems early, when changes are cheap and easy to make.

questions.q: A rough, cheap early model made from card or foam to test shape and size is best called a...
options: Orthographic drawing
Mock-up
Finished product
Working prototype
questions.explain: A mock-up is a simple, low-cost model (often card or foam) used to check overall shape, size and proportion early in the design process.

questions.q: Which tool is most useful for planning the order and timing of tasks when making a product?
options: A flow chart or Gantt-style production plan
A questionnaire
A mood board
A sketch of the final idea
questions.explain: A production plan such as a flow chart or Gantt chart sets out the sequence, timing and resources for each stage of making.

questions.q: When evaluating a prototype, the designer should mainly judge it against...
options: The colour of the packaging only
The price of a competitor's advert
The points in the design specification
How long the sketch took to draw
questions.explain: Objective evaluation compares the prototype against each measurable point of the specification to see how well the need has been met.

questions.q: A designer asks target users to try a prototype and give feedback. This is an example of...
options: Recycling the product
User testing to gather evaluation evidence
Anthropometric percentile calculation
Writing the design brief
questions.explain: Getting real users to try the prototype and comment gives valuable feedback that feeds the evaluation and the next iteration of the design.

questions.q: What does 'anthropometrics' mean?
options: The collection and use of measurements of the human body
The cost of manufacturing a product
The environmental impact of a product
The study of the strength of materials
questions.explain: Anthropometrics is the study and use of human body measurements (such as hand span or sitting height) so products fit the users comfortably.

questions.q: Designing a handle so it is comfortable and easy to grip and use is mainly an example of good...
options: Costing
Recycling
Ergonomics
Batch production
questions.explain: Ergonomics is about designing products to fit the people who use them, making them comfortable, safe and easy to use; anthropometric data supports this.

questions.q: When designing a product for a wide range of adults, a designer often uses data from about the 5th to the 95th percentile so that...
options: The product is as cheap as possible
Exactly 50 people are measured
Only the smallest 5 percent of people are considered
The product suits the great majority of the intended users
questions.explain: Designing to the 5th-95th percentile range means the product fits roughly 90 percent of users, covering most of the intended population comfortably.

questions.q: Which set correctly lists the '6 Rs' of sustainable design?
options: Reduce, Refill, Recycle, Return, Rethink, Reward
Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink, Repair
Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Remake, Restore, Reboot
Reuse, Resell, Recycle, Rename, Repair, Refund
questions.explain: The 6 Rs are Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repair and Recycle: a framework for reducing the environmental impact of products.

questions.q: A designer chooses parts that can be unscrewed and replaced when they wear out, rather than gluing the product shut. Which of the 6 Rs does this best support?
options: Refuse
Repair
Recycle
Reduce
questions.explain: Making a product easy to take apart and mend supports 'Repair', extending its life and reducing waste. Designing for disassembly also aids later recycling.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Design & Technology (0445) syllabus; Design Process
